section: The comparison itself / the ranking rationale - 'For a second option, and the drug to beat: plain lidocaine, already in the syringe'
sentence_as_it_stands: It has by far the largest body of evidence behind it, the least painful injection of any solution measured, and the only sting that can be taken all the way to body pH by buffering.
quote: The effect of the buffering of the lo … cal anesthetic solutions was a raising … of the pH toward a more physiologic … range of 7.0 to 7.4 (Table 1). … The amount of pain associated with … the infiltration of the local anesthetic … solutions was dramatically reduced by … buffering (Figure).
corrected_wording: It has by far the largest body of evidence behind it and the least painful injection of any solution measured. It is not the only one of these drugs whose solution has been brought into the physiological pH range and measured there: a randomised, prospective, double-blind, within-subject study of 25 volunteers injected buffered and unbuffered mepivacaine intradermally alongside the two lidocaine solutions, reported every buffered solution inside 7.0 to 7.4, and found the pain of infiltration far lower for the buffered member of all three pairs, with the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick not significantly different between the members of the mepivacaine pair (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545). The laboratory study already cited in this record on the bupivacaine page reports the same for mepivacaine on a precipitation endpoint (AlShammari 2025).
notes: This is a uniqueness statement inside the sentence that ranks plain lidocaine as the drug to beat, so part of the ordering rests on it. The paper's own three unbuffered solutions and three buffered solutions are reported with their measured pH in its Table 1, and the buffered mepivacaine sits in the physiological range alongside the buffered lidocaine solutions. Written here as what the study did and found, with nothing about how any solution was made: no agent, no ratio, no volumes. Two caveats worth keeping. First, this paper rated pain on a 0-to-10 scale, not the 100 mm scale the page's table uses, so the numbers do not belong on that table's scale. Second, within this paper the buffered mepivacaine pair scored numerically lower than the buffered lidocaine pair, but the three drugs were never compared against one another by any test, so that is not a measured reversal of 'the least painful injection of any solution measured' and is not claimed as one here.

section: The second reversal: bupivacaine
sentence_as_it_stands: **The mixture performs like the chloroprocaine, not like the bupivacaine.** Adding the ester cost **139 − 36 = 103 minutes**, a **74%** loss, and the combination was statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine on its own.
quote: Statistical analysis revealed that the difference in … duration of action between bupivacaine alone and … bupivacaine plus chloroprocaine was highly signifi- … cant (p c 0.001), and that the difference in duration … of action between bupivacaine-chloroprocaine mix- … ture and chloroprocaine alone was also significant (p … -=0.01).
corrected_wording: The mixture performs much more like the chloroprocaine than like the bupivacaine. Adding the ester cost 139 − 36 = 103 minutes, a 74% loss. The combination was not statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine on its own: the full text reports that comparison as significant as well (p < 0.01), beside p < 0.001 for the mixture against bupivacaine alone.
notes: The paper's abstract says only that the mixture was 'similar to' chloroprocaine alone; the page upgrades that to a null result, which the Results section contradicts. The same upgrade appears in this page's own source register ('significantly less than bupivacaine alone and statistically indistinguishable from chloroprocaine alone'), so it needs fixing in both places. The direction matters: the mixture lasted significantly longer than the ester alone, so the amide's contribution was greatly reduced rather than abolished, which bears on this page's 'destroys the amide's duration' wording and on the Ropivacaine page's 'effectively erased'.

section: Sources > What has no source
sentence_as_it_stands: The claim that bupivacaine is the most painful to inject of the seven agents on the comparison page. No study has compared all seven for injection pain intradermally, and the one that is cited for the claim found etidocaine worse.
quote: During these experiments, stinging was a common experience with all test solutions.
corrected_wording: The claim that bupivacaine is the most painful to inject of the seven agents on the comparison page. No study has compared all seven for injection pain intradermally. The study cited for the claim is Howe & Williams 1994 (PMID 8034840), which compared three of them at matched pH and found lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine most; it remains the only pH-matched comparison and has not been corroborated. The only other intradermal comparison of those same three agents recorded injection pain without matching pH and found stinging common to all test solutions, ranking none of them (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776).
notes: The sentence is correct as far as it goes, and the attribution is right: the paper cited for the etidocaine-worse finding is Howe & Williams 1994, not Morgan & Russell 1975 (verified in Europe PMC, EXT_ID:8034840, and against every citing passage in the record). What the sentence does not show is that a second human intradermal comparison of exactly those three agents exists, 19 years earlier, and that it reports injection pain as common to all solutions without separating them. So the one-study ranking is uncorroborated and the only independent look at the same three agents found no difference. Morgan & Russell 1975 is cited nowhere in the record: searches of Notion for the PMID, the DOI, 'Morgan 1975' and the title returned no hit, and the string 'Morgan' does not occur in the bupivacaine, mepivacaine, ropivacaine, comparison, wheal-literature or Reference-register pages.

section: What is still unknown
sentence_as_it_stands: Whether [dose figure omitted] really outlasts [dose figure omitted] in skin. The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration-duration relationship at higher strengths. The full text was not obtainable. What would settle it: reading Aps and Reynolds 1976 in full, or a modern repeat.
quote: The increase in duration of action with increased concentration was greater for bupivacaine and etidocaine as compared with lignocaine.
corrected_wording: Whether a stronger solution really outlasts a weaker one in skin. The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration-duration relationship at higher strengths; the full text was not obtainable. A second, independent human intradermal measurement points the same way as the abstract: in a double-blind weal study in four volunteers, half-recovery of pinprick lengthened with concentration more steeply for bupivacaine and etidocaine than for lignocaine, and the higher of the two bupivacaine strengths tested gave roughly twice the half-recovery time of the lower (76.5 +/- 8.0 min against 40.5 +/- 6.3 min; Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776). Reading Aps and Reynolds 1976 in full would still settle the three-strength question.
notes: The page's own open question is answered in the same direction by a study the page does not hold. Morgan & Russell fitted half-recovery time against log concentration for each agent (their fig. 3) and found the concentration/duration slopes for bupivacaine and etidocaine clearly steeper than lignocaine's, which is the relationship this entry says it cannot settle. Measured in intradermal weals on normal forearm skin in four healthy men, on a half-recovery rather than a full-recovery endpoint, which is why it narrows rather than closes the question. Concentrations are omitted per the brief; only the two duration values and their ratio are given.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: How long does each one last? > What a tenfold rise in concentration buys, in skin
sentence_as_it_stands: Willatts fitted a straight line to duration against the logarithm of concentration for each drug. Those slopes are the clearest statement anyone has of what concentration is worth in this tissue.
quote: A log-linear response … was assumed for the two … standard drugs and so only two points were estimated. … Three points are given for etidocaine.
corrected_wording: Willatts fitted a straight line to duration against the logarithm of concentration for each drug, and his is the only such set covering six agents at once. It is not the only set: a 1975 double-blind weal study fitted half-recovery time against log concentration for lignocaine, bupivacaine and etidocaine in four volunteers and found the slopes for bupivacaine and etidocaine clearly steeper than lignocaine's, so bupivacaine joins ropivacaine as an agent whose skin duration does rise appreciably with concentration (Morgan & Russell 1975, PMID 1138776).
notes: The page says this comparison 'decides more about how to inject than any ranking between drugs in this document', so a second data set bears directly on something practical. The conclusion drawn from Willatts carries its own scope ('For the six drugs Willatts timed') and is not wrong; the page also already flags ropivacaine as an exception. What is overstated is 'the clearest statement anyone has': a second human intradermal concentration-duration data set exists, it covers two drugs on this page (lidocaine/lignocaine and bupivacaine), and for bupivacaine it runs the other way from the six-drug rule. Morgan & Russell's own figures are half-recovery times, not full recovery, and rest on four subjects, so they are a weaker data set than Willatts's - but they are the only concentration-duration figures for intradermal bupivacaine that exist, and the page currently has none.

section: The seven papers nobody has pulled > item 4 (Padfield 1967)
sentence_as_it_stands: 4. **Padfield 1967.** *The intradermal local analgesic action of prilocaine. A controlled double-blind comparison with lignocaine and procaine.* Anaesthesia 22(4):556–61. PMID 6054556. **Unread; no abstract exists**, but its result is quoted in the 1985 paper: the three agents were "equi-analgesic shortly after injection, with **procaine having the shortest, and prilocaine the longest duration of action**," and there was a **60% incidence of vasodilatation with procaine**. **What the full text would settle:** the durations in minutes, and whether prilocaine's edge over lidocaine is large enough to matter.
quote: With the subject's eyes averted, each bleb was tested six times and the number of non-painful stimuli out of six were recorded and indicated the degree of analgesia. This assessment was repeated at 5, 10, 15,30 and 45 minutes.
corrected_wording: Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556) has now been read. It is a double-blind, Latin-square-randomised, saline-controlled within-subject comparison of prilocaine, lignocaine and procaine given as single intradermal blebs in 20 subjects, every solution without an added vasoconstrictor. It reports no duration for any agent: analgesia was scored as the number of non-painful pinpricks out of six at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30 and 45 minutes and summed into a 'Total Activity' score, and observation stopped at 45 minutes with all three agents still scoring above saline. On total activity prilocaine was more active than lignocaine (p < 0.05) and than procaine (p < 0.001), and lignocaine more active than procaine (p < 0.05). The 60% vasodilatation figure for procaine is confirmed at source: vasodilatation was noted by twelve of the twenty pairs. The quoted ranking 'procaine having the shortest, and prilocaine the longest duration of action' is the 1985 paper's gloss on that activity-over-time score; the full text contains no durations in minutes, so that part of the queue item cannot be settled by reading this paper.
notes: The queue item asks the full text for 'the durations in minutes'. The answer is that there are none: the paper measures analgesia scores at fixed times, not time to recovery. The stated aim does mention duration of action ('A group of 40 dental students participated in a double blind controlled trial ... with a view to assessing the activity and duration of action of procaine, lignocaine and prilocaine.', p2), which is probably why the 1985 paper paraphrased it as duration, but no duration value is reported anywhere in the paper.

section: Sources > the Foldes/Padfield CITATION ONLY entry
sentence_as_it_stands: **Foldes FF, McNall PG 1952**; and **Padfield A 1967**, *Anaesthesia* 22:556–561. — **`CITATION ONLY`**, both via Willatts & Reynolds 1985. Foldes: intradermal procaine and chloroprocaine duration in man **not prolonged by a plasma cholinesterase inhibitor**, with or without adrenaline, so in-situ ester hydrolysis does not determine intradermal duration (bears on 9.2). Padfield: prilocaine, [dose figure omitted] lignocaine and [dose figure omitted] procaine intradermally were equi-analgesic shortly after injection, with **procaine shortest and prilocaine longest in duration, and a 60% incidence of vasodilatation with procaine.** Neither read at source.
quote: A controlled double blind trial has shown that, intradermally, prilocaine [dose figure omitted] was a significantly more active local analgesic agent than lignocaine [dose figure omitted] and procaine [dose figure omitted]when total activity is measured over a 45 minute period as well as 30 and 45 minutes after its administration.
corrected_wording: Padfield A 1967, Anaesthesia 22:556-561 - read at source. A double-blind, Latin-square-randomised, saline-controlled within-subject comparison of prilocaine, lignocaine and procaine as single intradermal forearm blebs in 20 subjects, all without an added vasoconstrictor. The three agents scored close to maximal and close to each other at 0 to 10 minutes; over the whole 45 minutes prilocaine was more active than lignocaine (p < 0.05) and than procaine (p < 0.001), and lignocaine more active than procaine (p < 0.05). Vasodilatation with procaine in twelve of twenty pairs (60%) and vasoconstriction with prilocaine in eighteen of twenty. Limits: no duration of any kind is reported, so 'procaine shortest and prilocaine longest in duration' is the 1985 paper's gloss on an activity-over-time score; observation stopped at 45 minutes with analgesia still present in all three arms.
notes: 'Neither read at source' is now out of date for Padfield, and the duration wording carried into this record from Willatts and Reynolds should be replaced by the activity ranking the paper actually reports. The ranking's direction is right and statistically significant; the word duration is not supportable from the paper.

section: 9a.2 Two caveats, one of which the authors raise themselves > consequence
sentence_as_it_stands: `INFERENCE` **Consequence: their amide-versus-ester contrast survives intact, because both arms carried metabisulphite. Their amide-versus-saline comparison does not**, because the control was artificially dilated. When they say the amides produced “less vasodilatation than saline,” the saline in question was dilating three to six times more often than plain saline does. **Do not use this paper to claim lidocaine constricts skin relative to plain saline.**
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: One intradermal comparison of an amide against plain sodium chloride does exist, in a paper this page already cites second-hand. Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556) raised blebs of prilocaine, lignocaine, procaine and plain sodium chloride in the same forearm in each of 20 subjects, double-blind, with no metabisulphite in any solution; eighteen of the twenty pairs noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine relative to the saline control and twelve noticed vasodilatation with procaine. It is a naked-eye report at one concentration rather than a graded or instrumented measurement, and it covers prilocaine rather than lidocaine, so it does not settle whether lidocaine constricts skin relative to plain saline.
notes: This is the gap the page names - an amide against an uncontaminated saline control, intradermally, in humans - and the paper that partly fills it is the one already in this page's source list as CITATION ONLY. It fills it for prilocaine, not for lidocaine, and with naked-eye colour rather than grading or flowmetry, so the instruction not to read the lidocaine claim out of Willatts and Reynolds stands.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each one cost in injection pain? (the ropivacaine sentence that closes the 'A full buffer does not transfer to the other drugs' paragraph)
sentence_as_it_stands: No one has shown that a partly buffered ropivacaine stays clear, and any mixture is worth holding to the light before it is injected.
quote: Later, we determined the concen…tration of NaHCO3, which can be added to [dose figure omitted] of … [dose figure omitted] ropivacaine at room temperature, with and … without the previous addition of [dose figure omitted] adrenaline without provoking immediate … precipitation (5 minutes of optical microscope ob…servation) of the final anesthetic solution.
corrected_wording: A partly buffered ropivacaine has been shown to stay clear once, in the laboratory and over a short window. The laboratory phase of a randomised double-blind trial of lumbar peridural block in 60 patients located the point at which a precipitate appeared in ropivacaine, used a quantity below it, and reported no precipitate under an optical microscope over five minutes at room temperature; the same paper found precipitate in every solution recovered from rat tissue five minutes after injection, including the unmodified clinical-use preparation and most of all the alkalinised ones (Ramos 2001, PMID 11464357). Two laboratory studies report the opposite over longer windows or at larger bicarbonate quantities: precipitate still accumulating to a plateau at 20 minutes in a weaker ropivacaine at the lowest amount tried (Fulling & Peterfreund 2000, PMID 11009239), and precipitate at every bicarbonate volume tried (AlShammari 2025, PMID 40330160). A fourth put ropivacaine through its titration at its two strongest commercial strengths only, found precipitation above pH 6.0 and excluded it (Milner 2000, PMID 10758442). What no study has done is follow a partly buffered ropivacaine past a few minutes, or at the moment it enters tissue, and report it still clear.
notes: This is claim D017 and the sentence the whole open question was raised against; it is refuted as worded. Scope matters for how far the correction reaches. Ramos is a clinical peridural trial whose primary endpoints were block onset, spread and duration; the clarity observation was a laboratory step before the trial and an animal sub-study, never an inspection of the syringes given to patients - so the laboratory half of the sentence is settled and the clinical half is not. Milner 2000, the other full text read for this claim, is a pure laboratory solution study, which is exactly where it could have settled the question, and there ropivacaine precipitated at both strengths tested. Searched in Notion for 'Milner', 'Ramos', 'alkalinization', 'bicarbonate', 'precipitate', PMID 10758442, PMID 11464357, DOI 10.1046/j.1365-2346.2000.00596.x and DOI 10.1053/rapm.2001.24257 (engine: notion-search), and read the local copies of the ropivacaine, mepivacaine and bupivacaine wheal pages plus fresh fetches of this page, the Reference source register S1-S457, the Product Guide, '5 - Soft ground in these documents', 'What is still unsettled across these pages' and 'What was searched for and does not exist': Milner 2000, Ramos 2001 and Fulling 2000 are cited nowhere in the record, and the ropivacaine-buffering absence is not entered in the register of absences either. One loose end: a Letter/Comment on Ramos with an author reply exists (Lambert 2002, PMID 12016613) and is behind a subscription with no abstract, so it was not read.

section: The sting, and the two things that reduce it > 'A 2025 laboratory study put a number on the threshold' (the ropivacaine row of the AlShammari table); repeated in the Sources entry for AlShammari
sentence_as_it_stands: Ropivacaine | any volume | precipitated at every volume tested
quote: For solution B, this phenomenon … occurred with values of NaHCO3 ⭖ [dose figure omitted] and … for solution C, with values of NaHCO3 greater than
corrected_wording: Ropivacaine — tolerated none of the volumes tested — precipitated at every volume tested. The step size sets what that can mean: the study raised the buffer in fixed increments and its smallest increment was already several times larger than the quantity at which a precipitate first appeared in ropivacaine in an earlier laboratory determination, so the design could not have detected a window below that increment. Such a window was located and used: a laboratory phase fixed a quantity below the point at which a precipitate appeared and reported none under an optical microscope over five minutes at room temperature, and that solution was then given peridurally in a randomised double-blind trial in 60 patients (Ramos 2001, PMID 11464357). Two further limits belong with the 2025 row: its endpoint was visible precipitate, with no microscopy, and its report does not state which ropivacaine strength was tested (AlShammari 2025, PMID 40330160).
notes: The ropivacaine row is the figure that two pages lean on - the bupivacaine page's bupivacaine-versus-ropivacaine contrast and the comparison page's 'no one has shown' sentence - and as rendered it reads as a property of the drug rather than of the volumes tried. The 'any volume' cell in the 'Bicarbonate it tolerates' column also inverts the sense of the row: ropivacaine tolerated no volume tested, not any volume. The increment comparison is derived, not quoted, and the assumption is named here: the 2025 study's Europe PMC record (EXT_ID:40330160) gives its increment as a fixed volume step of the 8.4 per cent bicarbonate preparation, and at that strength the step works out several times the quantity at which Ramos first saw precipitate in 10 mL of its ropivacaine solution. Confirmed in the same record that 'Ropivacaine precipitated with all volumes of buffer' is the study's own sentence and that the ropivacaine strength is not stated in it, so the page quotes it accurately; the overstatement is in treating it as the whole of what is known.

page: 🔬 The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites, and the two conclusions it overturned
section: Sources — The Reynolds series (Reynolds F, Bryson THL, Nicholas ADG 1976 annotation); and the same paper's row in the seven-papers table
sentence_as_it_stands: Limits: abstract read; full text not indexed and not read. … No durations in minutes are available from the abstract, so the study establishes the absence of a concentration effect but not the durations of the comparators.
quote: TABLE III. Time to full recovery … Time (min) … Agent              n      Mean SEM
corrected_wording: Full text read. Table III tabulates the mean time to full recovery in minutes, with SEM and n, for every agent and concentration: in the first trial lignocaine 65.7 ± 5.3 (n=28), bupivacaine 82.5 ± 8.7 (n=28) and aptocaine 91.3 ± 2.8 pooled (n=167); in the second, prilocaine 78.6 ± 5.1 pooled (n=81), mepivacaine 98.6 ± 4.7 pooled (n=81) and aptocaine 98.9 ± 8.1 (n=27). Times to 50% recovery are given in the text: about 32 min for lignocaine, bupivacaine and prilocaine, 60 min for mepivacaine and aptocaine. The endpoint is a permanent score of 10, that is complete recovery of pinprick sensation over the bleb, tested every 10 min, at [dose figure omitted] per intradermal injection.
notes: This is the correction the rest of the packet turns on. Several pages state that no human intradermal head-to-head gives durations in minutes; this paper does, for five agents, and its full text is readable. Per-concentration means in minutes are also given for mepivacaine and prilocaine.

section: The recommendation (first bullet)
sentence_as_it_stands: The only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981).
quote: Every 10 min the area of … each bleb was tested five times with a lancet, while the … subject looked away, and the number of times out of … 10 that the prick felt sharp, for each solution, was … recorded. This was continued until sensation had … returned to normal at all sites.
corrected_wording: Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194) measured mepivacaine in human skin by that same test five years earlier — pinprick over an intradermal bleb, tested every 10 min to a permanent score of 10 — in 27 double-blind volunteers at three concentrations, giving mean times to full recovery of 97.0, 95.2 and 103.7 min (98.6 min pooled, n=81) and 60 min to 50% recovery. Three studies, not one, have measured mepivacaine in human skin by that test (Reynolds 1976; Fairley and Reynolds 1981; Willatts and Reynolds 1985), and all three put it under two hours.
notes: This is the page's headline recommendation sentence and the lead the S1 task flagged. The page's conclusion that mepivacaine is not a longer wheal survives; the uniqueness claim does not. The 1976 method section says of the second trial 'Exactly the same procedure was followed', so the pinprick-over-bleb method quoted here covers the mepivacaine arm.

section: What is still unknown ('Whether the square-root scaling holds'); and Why the eight-hour figure does not apply to a wheal / Sources › Duration in skin, where Sweet 1982 is called the governing number
sentence_as_it_stands: Whether the square-root scaling holds. The 60-minute estimate for a [dose figure omitted] wheal is an interpolation between two studies that differ in tissue layer, endpoint and country.
quote: The mean time to full recovery (permanent score of … 10) was calculated for each agent and is shown in table Ilia. The mean duration to full recovery for … aptocaine (all solutions) was significantly longer than … for lignocaine (P< 0.001) but not for bupivacaine.
corrected_wording: A third human intradermal measurement sits between the two the estimate interpolates from. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed plain bupivacaine in 28 double-blind volunteers, in skin, at a wheal volume, to complete recovery of pinprick sensation: mean 82.5 min (SEM 8.7). It shares the endpoint and the tissue layer with Sweet 1982 at half Sweet's volume, so the step between those two volumes can be read from measurement rather than interpolated.
notes: The page's own 'What would settle it' asks for wheals of three volumes timed side by side; two of the three now have a measurement with the same endpoint in the same tissue layer. Reynolds 1976 is not cited anywhere on this page.

section: The comparability argument ('The duration comparisons are at unmatched concentrations and in unmatched tissues')
sentence_as_it_stands: Only Cederholm 1994 compares two drugs at matched concentration, matched volume and matched route, and the two drugs are ropivacaine and bupivacaine
quote: Exactly the same procedure was followed. … Twenty-seven volunteers, aged 20-51 yr, seven of … whom participated in the previous study, received the … following seven solutions:
corrected_wording: Cederholm 1994 is not the only study comparing two drugs at matched concentration, matched volume and matched route. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) compared mepivacaine and prilocaine at three matched concentrations each, at the same intradermal volume and by the same route, in the same 27 volunteers in one session, timing duration to complete recovery: mepivacaine 98.6 ± 4.7 min pooled against prilocaine 78.6 ± 5.1 min, the difference significant at P<0.01. Cederholm remains the only matched comparison that includes ropivacaine.
notes: The page uses this sentence to argue that the duration comparisons cannot be ranked against each other. A matched-concentration, matched-volume, same-subject human intradermal duration comparison of two marketed agents does exist.

section: 9a.5 Mepivacaine — the drug nobody in this project has considered ('Would not: duration')
sentence_as_it_stands: Block potency 1.5 against ropivacaine’s 6, and in Willatts & Reynolds every mepivacaine bleb had fully recovered within 80 minutes.
quote: Mepivacaine [dose figure omitted]           27       97.0 ±9.0 … 27       95.2 ±7.6 … 103.7 ±7.7 … all       81       98.6 ±4.7

corrected_wording: It cannot be brought to body pH. Peterfreund, Datta and Ostheimer (1989, PMID 2562097) tested this on the bench: 2-chloroprocaine and lidocaine "readily alkalinized to near physiological pH without precipitation," mepivacaine showed delayed precipitation with an 18-to-20-minute latency at [dose figure omitted], and "bupivacaine and etidocaine solutions precipitated after the addition of small amounts of sodium bicarbonate and could not be alkalinized to physiologic pH." A second bench titration reaches the same place from the other direction and adds a detection limit. It carried three bupivacaine strengths and two bupivacaine-with-epinephrine solutions through a titration in triplicate, from three production batch numbers each, and found no precipitate by naked eye against white and black backgrounds, under high-power microscopy, after centrifugation, or after the samples had stood an hour. But it also reports that earlier work with particle counters recorded particle counts rising after alkalinisation of similar solutions above pH 7, where eye and microscope found nothing (Milner 2000, PMID 10758442). So every 'no visible precipitate' result on this page, including the 2025 series' visible-precipitate endpoint, is bounded by how closely the solution was looked at.

sentence_as_it_stands: That tradition is small, old and British, and the reviews do not read it. The core of it is five papers from one anesthetic unit at St Thomas' Hospital in London between 1976 and 1985, plus a scatter of American dermatology and anesthesia papers between 1952 and 1994.

section: Sources > the Padfield register entry
sentence_as_it_stands: **Padfield A.** The intradermal local analgesic action of prilocaine. A controlled double-blind comparison with lignocaine and procaine. *Anaesthesia* 1967;22(4):556–61. PMID 6054556. DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2044.1967.tb10153.x. — **Limits: unread. No abstract exists.** Its findings are known second-hand from Willatts and Reynolds 1985: the three agents were equi-analgesic shortly after injection, procaine had the shortest and prilocaine the longest duration, and procaine produced a 60% incidence of vasodilatation. No minutes. Indexed as a randomised controlled trial with *injections, intradermal*, in adults.
quote: A controlled double blind trial has shown that, intradermally, prilocaine [dose figure omitted] was a significantly more active local analgesic agent than lignocaine [dose figure omitted] and procaine [dose figure omitted]when total activity is measured over a 45 minute period as well as 30 and 45 minutes after its administration.
corrected_wording: Padfield A. The intradermal local analgesic action of prilocaine. A controlled double-blind comparison with lignocaine and procaine. Anaesthesia 1967;22(4):556-561. PMID 6054556. DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2044.1967.tb10153.x. - Read at source. Double-blind, Latin-square-randomised, saline-controlled within-subject comparison of prilocaine, lignocaine and procaine as single intradermal forearm blebs in 20 subjects, all solutions without an added vasoconstrictor; analgesia scored as non-painful pinpricks out of six at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30 and 45 minutes and summed as 'Total Activity'. Prilocaine more active than lignocaine (p < 0.05) and procaine (p < 0.001); lignocaine more active than procaine (p < 0.05); saline less active than the agents combined (p < 0.001). The 60% vasodilatation figure for procaine is confirmed (twelve of twenty pairs), and the paper adds that eighteen of twenty noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine. Limits: no duration of any kind is measured, so the 'procaine shortest, prilocaine longest duration' ranking is the 1985 paper's gloss on an activity-over-time score; observation ends at 45 minutes with analgesia still present; vascular effects are naked-eye reports, not graded or instrumented; 20 healthy dental students, forearm skin.
notes: 'Limits: unread. No abstract exists.' is now out of date for the unread half. Europe PMC confirms there is still no abstract, and confirms the author is Padfield alone - no second author.

page: What is still unsettled across these pages, and what would settle each one
section: Seven intradermal papers never pulled
sentence_as_it_stands: **Seven intradermal papers never pulled.** Swerdlow & Jones, *Br J Anaesth* 1970;42(4):335–9 — intradermal bupivacaine, prilocaine and lignocaine with and without adrenaline, the broadest early comparison, no PubMed abstract; Wightman & Vaughan, *Anesthesiology* 1976;45(6):687–9 — compounds for intradermal anaesthesia including benzyl alcohol, parabens, procaine, lidocaine and saline, the control-solution paper the benzyl alcohol result needs; Padfield, *Anaesthesia* 1967;22(4):556–61 — intradermal prilocaine against lignocaine against procaine, double-blind; Foldes & McNall, *Anesthesiology* 1952;13(3):287–96, DOI 10.1097/00000542-195205000-00009 — procaine and chloroprocaine intradermally in man with a plasma cholinesterase inhibitor; Defalque & Stoelting, *Anesth Analg* 1967;46(3):311–14 — latency and duration of the common agents; Kim et al, *Anesth Analg* 1979;58(5):386–8 — bupivacaine and chloroprocaine intradermal antagonism, which bears on whether an ester and an amide can be mixed; Moses et al, *J Drugs Dermatol* 2023;22(4):364–8 — a modern repeat of the injection-pain-and-duration comparison. **Limits:** none of the seven has been read. Foldes 1952 is open access as a scanned PDF and carries 29 citing statements with no editorial notices; the others were not obtained. This is the highest-value unopened material in the project, and the same kind of evidence has already overturned two conclusions in it.
quote: The double blind, controlled trial was carried out during a series of practical classes by twenty pairs of clinical dental students.
corrected_wording: Six intradermal papers never pulled. The Padfield 1967 entry is now read: Anaesthesia 1967;22(4):556-561, PMID 6054556 - a double-blind, Latin-square-randomised comparison of intradermal prilocaine against lignocaine against procaine with a plain saline control in 20 subjects, with no vasoconstrictor in any arm and no duration measured; analgesia was scored by pinprick at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30 and 45 minutes and summed. 'Limits: none of the other six has been read.'
notes: The entry's own description - 'intradermal prilocaine against lignocaine against procaine, double-blind' - is accurate; what changes is the count, the read/unread status, and the fact that this paper supplies no duration figure for the pages that want one.

section: Why epinephrine is not the lever here > item 3; and the table row 'Benefit from a vasoconstrictor'
sentence_as_it_stands: 3. **The one intradermal experiment that tested a vasoconstrictor against procaine specifically found no prolongation.** Foldes and McNall gave procaine and chloroprocaine by the intradermal route in man and found duration **not prolonged by a plasma cholinesterase inhibitor, with or without adrenaline**.
quote: The drugs used, prilocaine ([dose figure omitted]), lignocaine ([dose figure omitted]), procaine ([dose figure omitted]) (all without an added vasoconstrictor agent) and [dose figure omitted] sodium chloride solution were kindly supplied by the St Bartholomew's Hospital Dispensary in identical numbered bottles.
corrected_wording: No change needed. The one intradermal experiment that tested a vasoconstrictor against procaine specifically found no prolongation. Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), the only other human intradermal study of procaine against comparators, has been read and is not a second such test: every solution in it was given without an added vasoconstrictor, and no duration was measured.
notes: This sentence and the matching table cell were flagged uncertain pending this paper, on the possibility that it contained an adrenaline arm. It does not. Adrenaline appears in the paper only once, as an uninjected comparator for the blanching prilocaine produced, from the author's personal observation.

section: What is still unknown > 'What ends an intradermal procaine block'
sentence_as_it_stands: - **What ends an intradermal procaine block.** The vascular explanation rests on one 1952 paper read second-hand and on the vasodilatation seen in 1985. *What would settle it:* the Foldes and McNall primary text, and a modern intradermal study with laser Doppler flowmetry run past 90 minutes — no study has recorded skin blood flow at a wheal of any of these drugs for longer than that; the longer recordings are at a fingertip after a finger block and under the skin ([Ropivacaine Wheals](https://app.notion.com/p/2c010b7903aa83a0b9e3813036c9d26e), 4.11).
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: What ends an intradermal procaine block. The vascular explanation rests on one 1952 paper read second-hand and on intradermal vasodilatation observed in two separate human studies: Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), where vasodilatation with procaine was noted by twelve of the twenty pairs against a plain saline control raised in the same forearm, and Willatts and Reynolds 1985. What would settle it: the Foldes and McNall primary text, and a modern intradermal study with laser Doppler flowmetry run past 90 minutes.
notes: The vascular half of this explanation no longer rests on 1985 alone. Padfield's observation is eighteen years earlier, independent, and - unlike Willatts and Reynolds - was made against a plain sodium chloride control with no metabisulphite in any solution. It is a naked-eye report rather than a graded or instrumented measurement, which is worth stating alongside it.

section: What does each drug do to blood vessels in skin?
sentence_as_it_stands: Two older intradermal studies scored the colour of the skin at the injection site rather than instrumenting it, and both add something the flowmetry does not.
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: Three older intradermal studies scored the colour of the skin at the injection site rather than instrumenting it, and each adds something the flowmetry does not. The earliest is Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), in which eighteen of twenty pairs noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine and twelve noticed vasodilatation with procaine, relative to a plain sodium chloride control bleb raised in the same forearm.

Its vascular data are free-text reports by subjects and partners rather than a graded score at a fixed time, so it carries less weight than the 1981 and 1985 studies on grading while carrying more on the choice of control.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each drug do to blood vessels in skin? (prilocaine sentence)
sentence_as_it_stands: Prilocaine has less vasodilating activity than lidocaine, which is why it, like mepivacaine, can be used without a vasoconstrictor (*StatPearls*, 2025).
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: A primary human intradermal observation of prilocaine's effect on skin vessels exists: in Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), eighteen of twenty pairs noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine relative to a plain sodium chloride control bleb raised in the same forearm, and the author recorded that the blanching prilocaine produced was less marked than adrenaline's.
notes: The page sources prilocaine's vascular behaviour to a textbook (StatPearls) and states it only as less widening than lidocaine. The 1967 paper reports active narrowing in human skin at a higher concentration than Willatts and Reynolds tested, in 18 of 20 subjects. Padfield's comparison with adrenaline is a personal observation, not a trial arm, and the strength is omitted here.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: Which drug for which purpose? > procaine paragraph
sentence_as_it_stands: **No vasoconstrictor extends it meaningfully, and the reason is vascular rather than enzymatic.** The usual explanation is that procaine is destroyed on the spot by cholinesterase in the tissue — but if that were what ends the block, inhibiting the enzyme would lengthen it, and in the one intradermal test in man it did not: duration was **not prolonged by a plasma cholinesterase inhibitor, either with or without adrenaline**.
quote: The drugs used, prilocaine ([dose figure omitted]), lignocaine ([dose figure omitted]), procaine ([dose figure omitted]) (all without an added vasoconstrictor agent) and [dose figure omitted] sodium chloride solution were kindly supplied by the St Bartholomew's Hospital Dispensary in identical numbered bottles.
corrected_wording: No change needed. In the one intradermal test in man, duration was not prolonged by a plasma cholinesterase inhibitor, either with or without adrenaline. Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556) has been read and does not add a second intradermal test of a vasoconstrictor on procaine: no solution in it contained a vasoconstrictor and it reports no duration.
notes: Checked because this sentence was flagged uncertain pending Padfield. The sentence stands. Note separately that Padfield did rank intradermal procaine least active of the three agents it tested, which is consistent with the page's 'short' characterisation while supplying no minutes.

section: What is not known (first bullet)
sentence_as_it_stands: **Nobody has timed a prilocaine wheal in human skin beyond the one intradermal study above, which says only that every injection had recovered completely by 80 minutes and gives no mean per concentration** (Willatts and Reynolds, 1985).
quote: With the subject's eyes averted, each bleb was tested six times and the number of non-painful stimuli out of six were recorded and indicated the degree of analgesia. This assessment was repeated at 5, 10, 15,30 and 45 minutes.
corrected_wording: At least two other human intradermal studies have tested prilocaine blebs serially over time: Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), which scored pinprick analgesia at 0, 5, 10, 15, 30 and 45 minutes in 20 subjects with analgesia still present when observation ended, and Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194). Neither reports a mean duration per concentration, so the measurement the page wants - a recovery time per concentration in human skin - still does not exist.
notes: The conclusion of the bullet survives; the wording 'Nobody has timed a prilocaine wheal in human skin beyond the one intradermal study above' does not. Padfield timed one serially in 1967 but his observation window closed before recovery, so no duration can be read from it.

section: Where does prilocaine sit among the local anesthetics? > second point
sentence_as_it_stands: **It widens skin blood vessels less than lidocaine does.** Lidocaine relaxes the muscle cells in the walls of small vessels, which widens them and increases blood flow — and since removal is proportional to blood flow, a drug that widens the vessels around itself speeds up its own removal. Prilocaine has less of this widening effect, which is one reason it can be used without a **vasoconstrictor**, meaning a drug such as epinephrine added specifically to narrow those vessels and slow the removal (*StatPearls*, 2025).
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: A primary human observation exists for this: in Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556), a double-blind intradermal comparison in 20 subjects, eighteen of twenty pairs noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine relative to a plain sodium chloride control bleb in the same forearm, and twelve noticed vasodilatation with procaine. The author recorded the blanching prilocaine produced as less marked than adrenaline's.
notes: The page's mechanism for prilocaine's standing rests on a textbook entry describing less widening than lidocaine. The 1967 paper reports narrowing rather than reduced widening, in human skin, at a higher concentration than the intradermal study the page relies on for duration. No recommendation follows from it and none is implied here.

section: 9a.3 Procaine, specifically > point 1
sentence_as_it_stands: `ABSTRACT-ONLY` Padfield 1967, cited in the same discussion, found a **60% incidence of vasodilatation with [dose figure omitted] procaine** intradermally in volunteers.
quote: Of the twenty pairs, eighteen noticed vasoconstriction occurring with priIocaine relative to the saline control and vasodilatation was noted by twelve with procaine.
corrected_wording: Verified at source. Padfield 1967 (PMID 6054556) reports that vasodilatation was noted by twelve of the twenty pairs with procaine - 60% - at intradermal blebs in 20 subjects, against a plain sodium chloride control bleb in the same forearm. The same sentence adds that eighteen of the twenty pairs noticed vasoconstriction with prilocaine.
notes: The 60% figure and the concentration attributed to Padfield are both correct. The ABSTRACT-ONLY / CITATION ONLY tag can become FULLTEXT; there is no abstract, but the full text has now been read. The procaine figure is a count of pairs reporting a free-text observation, not a graded score.

section: PART VI — MIXING, AND THE PROCAINE PROBLEM > 9.3 pH decides the outcome of a mixture (the closing INFERENCE)
sentence_as_it_stands: A [dose figure omitted] ampoule is acidic; diluting it with unbuffered normal saline changes the pH in a direction nobody has characterised for this route.
quote: The variables pH, PCO2, and nonionized fraction of the patients in group G1 did not present statistically significant differences … before and after the addition of [dose figure omitted] NaCl.
corrected_wording: A ropivacaine ampoule is acidic, and the direction has now been characterised in the solution, though still not for this route. A peridural trial used ropivacaine diluted with unbuffered normal saline as its control solution and measured pH, PCO2 and the nonionized fraction before and after the addition, in three lots of the anaesthetic and in its 20-patient control arm: none of the three changed significantly, and the solution did not precipitate at room temperature (Ramos 2001, PMID 11464357). So what remains unmeasured is this route, not the direction of the pH change itself.
notes: Section 9.3's wider point - that pH is an uncontrolled variable across the literature - is untouched, and the route qualifier keeps the sentence from being wrong. What the sentence overstates is the chemistry: the pH effect of adding unbuffered normal saline to this exact anaesthetic has been measured, twice over (bench lots and a patient arm), and the answer is no significant change. The sentence also sits next to the record's own note that Moffitt raised pH as the explanation for an anomalous pain result when diluting with unbuffered saline, so the measured null is directly relevant to that explanation. Section 9.3 is otherwise about mixing with other local anaesthetics rather than about bicarbonate, and neither Ramos nor any of the bicarbonate-in-ropivacaine literature appears anywhere on this page.

section: PART VIII — PRACTICAL > 11.2 (the third caution, precipitation); and the 2026-09-19 correction-log entry that added it
sentence_as_it_stands: A third caution, precipitation. Section 2.3 of the US Naropin label, read in the label's own words on 2026-09-19 (the rest of the label was not read here), says ropivacaine's solubility is limited above pH 6, so it may precipitate if mixed with alkaline solutions, and that a solution showing particles or discolouration should not be given.
quote: In the popliteal foss…sae of the rats, all of the solutions, including the one … prepared for clinical use, precipitated. This was … most evident in the alkalinized solutions.
corrected_wording: A third caution, precipitation. Section 2.3 of the US Naropin label says ropivacaine's solubility is limited above pH 6, so it may precipitate if mixed with alkaline solutions, and that a solution showing particles or discolouration should not be given. Four published studies have put sodium bicarbonate into ropivacaine and reported what became of the solution, and none is cited on this page. A laboratory determination found a quantity below the point at which a precipitate appeared and reported none over five minutes, gave that solution peridurally to patients, and found precipitate in every solution recovered from rat tissue after injection, including the unmodified clinical-use preparation (Ramos 2001, PMID 11464357). A bench study measured precipitate accumulating to a plateau at 20 minutes at the lowest amount tried in a weaker ropivacaine (Fulling & Peterfreund 2000, PMID 11009239). A 2025 laboratory series reported precipitate at every volume tried (AlShammari 2025, PMID 40330160). A titration tested ropivacaine at its two strongest commercial strengths only and found precipitation above pH 6.0 (Milner 2000, PMID 10758442). The pH threshold the label names is the figure all four converge on, and the animal finding is the one thing none of the others reports.
notes: The caution itself is right and the label is quoted correctly; what is understated is its footing. On this page the precipitation evidence is a label sentence plus one incidental - ropivacaine precipitating in Krebs' bicarbonate buffer in a 1993 dog-vessel study (Nakamura, section 4.9) - while four studies exist whose whole subject is bicarbonate in ropivacaine. The Ramos animal result is the only published observation of ropivacaine precipitating after it has entered tissue, and it did so for the unmodified clinical-use preparation as well as the buffered ones, which is a different and broader fact than the label's mixing warning. Recorded as an addition to the footing, not as a change to what the caution says.

section: How long does a mepivacaine block actually last? › In skin, which is the tissue that matters here
sentence_as_it_stands: Two studies have measured this, four years apart, from the same laboratory, and they agree. … Between them they cover 33 volunteers, and neither found a mepivacaine bleb lasting more than two hours.
quote: Mepivacaine [dose figure omitted]           27       97.0 ±9.0 … 27       95.2 ±7.6 … 103.7 ±7.7 … all       81       98.6 ±4.7
corrected_wording: Three studies have measured this, from the same laboratory over nine years, and they agree. Between them they cover 60 volunteers, and none found a mepivacaine bleb lasting more than about 1.7 hours — the longest group mean in the earliest of them, Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194), being 103.7 ± 7.7 min.
notes: Reynolds 1976 adds 27 volunteers and is the earliest of the three, not a later one; the page's substantive conclusion is unchanged and in fact strengthened.

section: Sources › Skin: vessels and duration (Willatts & Reynolds 1985 annotation)
sentence_as_it_stands: The second intradermal measurement of mepivacaine, and the only one that times it against lidocaine and prilocaine in the same volunteers.
quote: Exactly the same procedure was followed. … Twenty-seven volunteers, aged 20-51 yr, seven of … whom participated in the previous study, received the … following seven solutions:
corrected_wording: The third intradermal measurement of mepivacaine, and the only one that times it against lidocaine and prilocaine together in the same volunteers. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) timed mepivacaine against prilocaine in the same 27 volunteers in one session, but lignocaine was injected in a separate earlier trial in a different group of 28, so Reynolds 1976 is not a mepivacaine-versus-lidocaine comparison in the same subjects.
notes: The point the S1 task asked to settle. Reynolds 1976 ran two trials with different subject groups (seven subjects overlapped): trial 1 was lignocaine, bupivacaine and aptocaine in the same 28 subjects; trial 2 was mepivacaine, prilocaine and aptocaine in the same 27. No agent except aptocaine crosses the two trials, so any 'same volunteers' comparison drawn from this paper must stay inside one trial.

section: Sources › Skin: vessels and duration (Fairley & Reynolds 1981 annotation)
sentence_as_it_stands: The load-bearing source on this page and the larger of the two measurements of mepivacaine in human skin
quote: Mepivacaine [dose figure omitted]           27       97.0 ±9.0 … 27       95.2 ±7.6 … 103.7 ±7.7 … all       81       98.6 ±4.7
corrected_wording: The load-bearing source on this page, and one of three measurements of mepivacaine in human skin. Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194) used 27 volunteers against Fairley's 23, so Fairley is not the larger; it remains the one that maps the widest concentration range and the only one reporting the isomers separately.

section: What is not known (first item, 'How long a mepivacaine wheal lasts on these legs')
sentence_as_it_stands: Duration in human skin has been measured once, by Fairley and Reynolds, on forearms of healthy volunteers in their twenties, at half-recovery rather than full block.
quote: TABLE III. Time to full recovery … Time (min) … Agent              n      Mean SEM
corrected_wording: Duration in human skin has been measured three times. The earliest, Reynolds 1976 (PMID 776194), used a full-recovery endpoint — a permanent score of 10 on pinprick over the bleb — on the flexor forearms of volunteers aged 20 to 51, giving 98.6 ± 4.7 min pooled for mepivacaine (n=81). What is still unmeasured is a mepivacaine wheal in neuropathic leg skin.
notes: Two errors in one sentence: 'measured once' and 'at half-recovery rather than full block'. A full-recovery endpoint in human skin does exist for mepivacaine. The page's 'What would settle it' — a same-day leg-against-leg comparison — remains unmet.

section: What is still unknown ('Whether [dose figure omitted] really outlasts [dose figure omitted] in skin')
sentence_as_it_stands: The abstract of the one study that tested three strengths says it does; the same authors' later description of their own work says there is no concentration–duration relationship at higher strengths. The full text was not obtainable.
quote: there is no significant difference in duration … between the three different concentrations of … mepivacaine and prilocaine.
corrected_wording: A separate Reynolds-group paper from the same year and the same journal volume bears on this without settling it: Reynolds, Bryson and Nicholas 1976 (PMID 776194, Br J Anaesth 48:347-354, a different paper from Aps and Reynolds at 48:1171-1174) tested three concentrations each of three agents intradermally in human volunteers and found no significant difference in duration between them, which matches the authors' later description of a flat concentration-duration relationship at the higher strengths. It gave bupivacaine at one concentration only, so the question of the two bupivacaine strengths is still open.
notes: Also a citation hazard worth recording: there are two Reynolds-group 1976 papers in Br J Anaesth volume 48 — the aptocaine intradermal trial at 48:347 and Aps and Reynolds on concentration and vasoactivity at 48:1171. They should not be conflated.

section: 9a.5 Mepivacaine — the drug nobody in this project has considered (concentration–duration slope bullet)
sentence_as_it_stands: It had the steepest concentration–duration slope of the six (31.12 min per log unit).

section: Literature - ropivacaine's intrinsic cutaneous vasoconstriction > What the cited studies establish about duration
sentence_as_it_stands: No cited study measured skin blood flow beyond 90 minutes. The three primary studies stop at 30 minutes, 90 minutes, and an unreported endpoint, respectively. The evidence therefore cannot determine whether ropivacaine's effect on skin blood flow lasts two, four, or six hours.
quote: skin perfusion values reached +160.2% (p = 0.008) after 56 minutes and +129.7% (p = 0.01) after 6 hours. … 24 hours after injection the acral perfusion reduced to +35.1% (p = 0.03) in comparison to the initial perfusion values before injection (Table 2).
corrected_wording: No study cited on this page measured skin blood flow beyond 90 minutes: the three primary studies stop at 30 minutes, 90 minutes and an unreported endpoint. Those studies cannot determine whether ropivacaine's effect on skin blood flow lasts two, four or six hours. Evidence beyond 90 minutes does exist by a different route: after a plain-ropivacaine digital nerve block, finger skin perfusion was still raised at 6 hours and at 24 hours in two randomised double-blind volunteer studies (Häfner 2008, PMID 18334782; Schnabl 2013, PMID 23076005). Those are nerve blocks with the probe away from the injection site, not intradermal or subcutaneous wheals, so they do not settle the question for this page's route.
notes: The first two sentences are correctly scoped to the page's own citations. The third generalises to 'the evidence' and is too broad: the question it calls undecidable has an answer by the digital-block route, and the answer runs the opposite way to this section's heading - plain ropivacaine at the strength used was vasodilatative for 6 hours and still measurably raised at 24. section: How long does it actually last? (opening paragraph)
sentence_as_it_stands: Longer than lidocaine in direction, and small in size once the tissue is right. Five measurements put numbers on it and they do not agree with each other, which is itself the finding. The one taken in human skin at a wheal volume is the one that decides it, and it is short.

Its point estimates run against the 'longer than lidocaine in direction' opening, while its significance test agrees with the page's own conclusion that the two are the same drug for practical purposes here.

It is four successive double-blind trials of 20 female volunteers each, timing intradermal skin weals on the ventral left forearm to the return of some sensation and to complete recovery: bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine each with and without adrenaline; the same three agents with adrenaline from hospital-prepared multidose vials against commercial ampoules; the three agents at double strength; and intradermal saline with and without adrenaline (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).

section: The recommendation ('Mepivacaine is not the longer wheal it looks like'); and 'How long does a mepivacaine block actually last? > In skin, which is the tissue that matters here'
sentence_as_it_stands: The only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981).
quote: the diameter of the area of the … skin anesthetized to pinprick was … identified and marked on the tape. … Measures of skin anesthe … sia were carried out for 4V2 minutes.
corrected_wording: The study that mapped it across concentrations in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981). It is not the only study to have pricked the skin over a mepivacaine bleb: this page's own second source timed recovery the same way (Willatts and Reynolds, 1985), and a randomised double-blind study of 25 volunteers marked the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick around an intradermal mepivacaine wheal, though only across the first few minutes, so it yields no duration (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545).
notes: Two separate points, one of which answers the question put to this paper. First, 'the only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use' is broader than the duration point it supports, and the page itself says two paragraphs later that two studies have measured this; a third study pricked the skin over a mepivacaine wheal without timing it. Second, and this is what the paper settles: W-M001 says the only study measuring mepivacaine in human skin by pinprick over an intradermal bleb is Fairley and Reynolds 1981, and this paper did measure mepivacaine in human skin by pinprick over an intradermal wheal, but it did not measure duration. It recorded the area insensitive to pinprick at six readings inside the first 4 1/2 minutes and then stopped, with that area still rising at the last reading, so it adds a human intradermal pinprick measurement of mepivacaine and no duration figure at all. Its abstract's phrase 'duration of skin anesthesia' is therefore not a measurement it made, which is worth recording so the abstract is not read as a third skin duration. How many studies have timed mepivacaine in skin is settled from Reynolds 1976, not from here.

section: What does each drug do to blood vessels in skin? (final paragraph); and What would settle what is unresolved ('What happens to skin blood flow at a wheal after the first ninety minutes?') - claim D000
sentence_as_it_stands: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a wheal of any of these drugs for longer than ninety minutes. The longer recordings were made elsewhere: ropivacaine at the fingertip for 24 hours after a block at the base of the finger, where it raised flow and kept it raised (Häfner et al., 2008), and lidocaine and bupivacaine under the skin for 6 hours, where flow was back to baseline by 30 minutes (Liu et al., 1995).
quote: A two-injection dorsal technique digital nerve block for local anesthesia of the finger nerve bundles (Oberst's-method anaesthetic block) was performed on index and ring finger of both hands in each volunteer at the base of the fingers. … After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes.
corrected_wording: No study has recorded skin blood flow at a wheal of any of these drugs for longer than ninety minutes. The longer recordings were made elsewhere: ropivacaine in the finger for 24 hours after a block at the base of the finger, in two studies from the same department, where it raised flow and kept it raised (Häfner 2008, PMID 18334782, read at the fingertip; Schnabl 2013, PMID 23076005, read on the back of the finger below the nail), and lidocaine and bupivacaine under the skin for 6 hours, where flow was back to baseline by 30 minutes (Liu et al., 1995).
notes: The leading sentence is correct and the paper does not disturb it - a digital nerve block is not a wheal, and the flow probe sat remote from the injection. Only the list of longer recordings is incomplete. Low rather than medium because nothing downstream turns on the count.

section: PART I > 4.11 What remains unmeasured about vessels, item 2 ('Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes'); and PART XI > 14. The rejected-claims table, row 'Nobody has recorded ropivacaine skin flux past 90 minutes'
sentence_as_it_stands: Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes. Cederholm's recordings stop there. The nearest thing is Häfner 2008, which followed [dose figure omitted] ropivacaine flux for 24 hours - but at a fingerpad after an Oberst block, where the injection is at the digit base and the measurement at the pad, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site.
quote: A two-injection dorsal technique digital nerve block for local anesthesia of the finger nerve bundles (Oberst's-method anaesthetic block) was performed on index and ring finger of both hands in each volunteer at the base of the fingers. … After in following 12 measurement points (before injection, 1, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 60, 360, 1440 minutes), in total the measurement period was 1440 minutes.
corrected_wording: Flux at a ropivacaine wheal beyond 90 minutes. Cederholm's recordings stop there. There are two nearest things, not one, both from the same department and both after an Oberst block rather than at a wheal: Häfner 2008 (PMID 18334782) followed flux at the fingerpad for 24 hours, and Schnabl 2013 (PMID 23076005) followed it on the back of the finger below the nail at 12 points out to 24 hours. In both the injection is at the digit base and the measurement away from it, so the needle trauma is not at the measurement site, and neither is a wheal.
notes: The gap itself is unchanged and the section's own conclusion - narrow the claim to 'at a wheal' - is correct. Only the count of near misses is short, and Schnabl is the one of the two whose schedule is now primary-verified.
